transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-28 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~60 mins | Attendees: Lena Park, Omar Singh (Redwood); Priya Raman, Tom Alvarez, Sarah Lee (Acme)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, we are gonna focus on throughput tuning — continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, token limits, and how KV cache and quantization affect throughput. Omar will lead the deep bits.

[00:18] Priya Raman: Thanks Lena. Our big constraint is hitting P95 <= 180ms for the short chat flows, but we also have a high-burst use case where cost matters. We want guidance on where to dial knobs without hurting tail latency.

[00:35] Omar Singh: Great. Quick note: transcription may be off on some acronyms, so sorry if I say KV cash or something — it's KV cache. Our approach is to think about three levers: batching, scheduler policy (max_num_seqs, max_tokens, preemption), and model variants/quantization.

[00:50] Tom Alvarez: One constraint — we run in our VPC for now, staging only. If we do Dedicated we'll move to Redwood Dedicated, but initial tests are in VPC. Also, we have long context requests up to 2k tokens.

[01:05] Omar: Ok, good. On continuous batching: Redwood's runtime maintains a batching window to aggregate in-flight sequences. The critical knobs are max_num_seqs (how many concurrent sequences are grouped) and max_total_tokens (to avoid super long single batches). For example, increasing max_num_seqs from 8 to 32 increases throughput up to the point you saturate GPU memory or kernel-launch overhead.

[01:28] Priya: Are there default safe values? We don't want to OOM during the staged runs.

[01:33] Omar: Defaults are conservative: max_num_seqs=8, max_tokens_per_batch=4096 total. For 2k token per request workloads, you might want max_num_seqs=12-16 and a max_total_tokens ~ 24k-32k. But you also need to watch sequence length variance — if many requests are near 2k, fewer sequences per batch fit.

[01:55] Sarah Lee: From security side: when running in our VPC, we need to ensure metrics and logs don't leak. We'll check the ACLs, but any tuning that generates profiling traces — how are those handled?

[02:06] Lena: We will only share aggregated perf traces; raw requests can be redacted. Omar will include notes on telemetry knobs.

[02:12] Omar: Back to scheduler: the runtime has a fast-path scheduler that prefers latency-sensitive queues. You can set priority buckets: low-latency vs high-throughput. For low-latency, set a smaller batch timeout and lower max_num_seqs; for throughput, increase those. Also there's a preemption threshold — long-running batches can be preempted by latency traffic.

[02:40] Tom: How do we test preemption behavior? We often have a mix of short chat requests and long summarization jobs.

[02:47] Omar: In the staging benchmark we'll run mixed workloads: 80% short (<=64 tokens), 20% long (>=1k tokens). We'll instrument request tagging so scheduler treats them differently. We'll show how to mark latency-critical routes in the config.

[03:05] Priya: KV cache — we use caching heavily for instruction-following flows. How does that factor into batching and memory?

[03:12] Omar: KV cache is per-session key/value state kept in GPU memory for fast autoregressive decoding. It reduces compute per token but increases memory footprint. If you have many warm sessions with huge KV caches, that reduces the headroom for big batch sizes. Two tips: 1) shard/cache eviction policies — set a TTL on KV cache entries for interactive sessions; 2) prefer smaller max_num_seqs when many sessions have large KV caches. We'll include a tuning section in the doc.

[03:42] Sarah: Any impact of quantization on latency? We saw some models get slower after 4-bit quantization in past tests.

[03:49] Omar: Good point. Quantization can reduce memory and increase throughput, but kernel implementation matters. On some GPUs, INT8/4-bit kernels have higher per-token latency for short sequences due to dequant/quant overhead. For high-throughput long sequences, quantization wins. We'll recommend running A/B benchmarks per model: full-fp16 vs q4 and q8. We'll attach prior benchmarks as a starting point.

[04:12] Lena: I'll share a short benchmark sheet and the tuning playbook after the call.

[04:18] Tom: About token limits: we have a 2k production limit but some requests spike to 5k. If someone hits 5k, what happens to batching?

[04:25] Omar: If a single request has 5k tokens, the scheduler will cap batches by max_total_tokens, so you might end up with single-request batches which have bad throughput. For that use case, you can do two things: 1) enforce request-level token limits (reject or truncate), 2) run those large jobs on a separate queue with dedicated nodes optimized for long contexts (Dedicated pools).

[04:48] Priya: Makes sense. For cost optimization, is there a recommended binning strategy for queues? E.g., short, medium, long contexts?

[04:55] Omar: Yes — short (<=128 tokens) low-latency pool with small batch_timeout (4-8ms), medium (128-1024) mixed pool, and long (>1024) dedicated throughput pool. Also use auto-scaling policies per pool so long-context nodes can spin up only when needed.

[05:14] Tom: On engineering effort: how invasive is the change to mark routes and set queue priorities? We want minimal code changes.

[05:20] Omar: Minimal — it's mostly config in the Redwood route definitions: route.profile = "low_latency" or "throughput". We will provide a sample helm/manifest snippet for the VPC connector and route tagging.

[05:35] Priya: About metrics, we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route P95/P99. Does Redwood expose that in VPC mode?

[05:43] Lena: Yes, in Private and Dedicated we expose token-level cost and latency via the console and via push metrics into your Prometheus or DataDog. For VPC/on-prem there are options for pushing metrics to your endpoints. Omar will document the Prometheus scrape config.

[06:00] Sarah: Compliance concern: SOC2 and audit logs for changes to scheduler/tuning — we need immutable logs for config changes.

[06:07] Lena: We keep config change audit logs in the control plane and can integrate with your SIEM. For Private deployments we can also provide offline export. We'll include security docs.

[06:18] Omar: I'll walk through a sample benchmark plan: 1) baseline: default config with 8 seqs, timeout 10ms; 2) throughput-first: max_num_seqs=24, timeout 25ms; 3) mixed queues with preemption on. We'll look at tokens/sec, P95 latency, and cost per 1M tokens.

[06:40] Priya: Any gotchas for mixed workloads and KV cache warmups? Our live traffic has session stickiness so warm cache tests matter.

[06:47] Omar: Yeah — warm-up matters. Include a warm-up phase in the benchmark where you replay a subset of production sessions to populate KV cache. Otherwise throughput numbers will look different. We suggest a 10-minute warmup at production QPS.

[07:05] Tom: For on-prem / air-gapped scenarios, can the tuning knobs be applied the same way?

[07:11] Omar: Yes — the runtime is identical. The main difference is telemetry and automatic kernel updates. For on-prem you'll manage the kernel binaries, but config parameters are the same. We'll provide install notes.

[07:24] Priya: Are there sample configs we can copy?

[07:27] Omar: Yes — I'll drop three sample YAMLs: low-latency, throughput, and mixed. Also a script to sweep max_num_seqs and batch_timeouts and report ops/sec and P95.

[07:40] Sarah: We'll need to loop legal on the dedicated pilot if we move beyond staging — any inputs from you on required contract clauses for dedicated pools?

[07:47] Lena: We'll have sales provide the Dedicated MSA checklist; for this sync we'll focus on tech. I'll flag procurement.

[07:55] Tom: Quick question on GPU memory: how do we estimate batch size given model, sequence length and KV cache? Any tooling?

[08:02] Omar: We have a memory estimator script that takes model size, quantization mode, avg seq length, and number of concurrent sessions and returns rough peak memory. I'll include that and sample outputs for a 7B fp16 and q4 model at 2k context. Expect larger mem for longer KV caches.

[08:20] Priya: Would be great to see a sample run with 2k token requests and mixed short traffic.

[08:25] Omar: That's part of the benchmark plan. We'll run two runs: one with cold cache and one warm cache. Also test q4 vs fp16 to compare throughput and tail latency.

[08:36] Lena: Ok let's recap next steps — Omar will send playbook and scripts, Tom will set up VPC staging access, Priya will send SLOs and traffic histogram. We'll run benchmarks and meet in two weeks.

[08:50] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks Omar and Lena.

[08:54] Omar: Thanks all — I'll also attach prior Redwood benchmarks (small sample) and a link to the tuning doc in the follow-up email: https://redwood.ai/tuning/playbook (note: placeholder link).

[09:02] Lena: Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcription had a few mis-hearings (e.g., KV cache -> KV cash, q4 -> cue four) and some speaker attribution was manual-corrected.
